summary.text:
The largest book we have read, and the one where a single undecided question is worth the most. Woking carries £2,185.4m at a weighted 3.06%, against a borough its size. There is no CFR in this report — the accounts were still being prepared — so nothing about internal borrowing can be said, and we say nothing.

What can be said is the shape, because we hold all 199 of their PWLB loans. 124 of them, £1.617bn, mature twenty-five years or more out at a weighted 2.564%; 72 are annuities at 2.303%. Sitting on top is £415.9m maturing inside twelve months at 4.502% — which ties to the 4.51% average they report for the year's new borrowing. Every year around £420m has to be found again at whatever the one-year rate is. At today's 4.95% that is about £1.86m a year more than last time.

The live item is paragraph 6.6: the Government confirmed an initial £500m tranche of debt relief in October 2025 and "the individual loans to be extinguished are still to be announced". The two halves of the book are worth wildly different amounts — on the DMO's curve this afternoon the long annuities are around £616m in discount while the one-year money is at par. Which loans go is a computable question and it is still open.

officer.body:
Hi Mike,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the annual report that went to Executive on 9 July, ahead of the mid-year report in the autumn. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first. We hold 199 PWLB loans for Woking. The balance we carry today is £2,085.4m against the £2,160.4m in your paragraph 9.1 table, and the two aren't meant to tie: ours amortises the annuities to today and picks up what has rolled since 31 March. What does tie is the price of the rollover. The 44 loans in our file maturing inside twelve months come to £415.9m at a weighted 4.502%, against the 4.51% average you report at 8.1 for the year's new borrowing. That's close enough that we're confident we're looking at the same book.

The shape is the thing. 124 of the 199 loans — £1.617bn — mature twenty-five years or more out at a weighted 2.564%, and 72 of those are annuities at 2.303%. That is roughly three-quarters of the book at a rate nobody can buy today. Above it sits the £415.9m of one-year money at 4.50%, which is the £427.43m you refinanced last year in a slightly different guise. One-year certainty closed at 4.95% this afternoon on notice 314/26. Replacing that bucket at today's rate rather than last year's is about £1.86m a year. That isn't a forecast and it isn't advice — it's just what the arithmetic says on 14 August, and it moves every day, which is the whole argument for watching it daily rather than at the next report. Our monthly sector breakdown at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity is the other half of it: July was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%, so you can see how much appetite is in the market before you need it.

Then paragraph 6.6, which is the reason we wrote. The £500m initial tranche is confirmed but "the individual loans to be extinguished are still to be announced". Those two halves of the book are worth very different amounts. On the DMO's premature repayment curve this afternoon the long annuities are deep in discount — the single largest, PW508481, £73.4m of remaining principal at 2.52% running to February 2069, prices about £27.5m below its balance — while the one-year money sits at par. Across the 182 loans we can schedule, the book carries something like £616m of discount in total. We're not suggesting what should happen with any of it; we don't sell treasury products and we're in no position to have a view. But if the composition of the £500m is genuinely still open, the difference between taking it from the 2.56% bucket and the 4.50% bucket is large, and it is computable. We compute it every morning for every council in the country; yours is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. Ours is indicative — the DMO's is the only quote that binds.

One disclosure on our own numbers, because we'd rather you heard it from us. We can schedule 182 of the 199 loans; the other 17, £162.8m, our file dates as already matured, so they drop out of everything above. If the maturity profile in your Appendix 2 says something different from our £415.9m, we'd genuinely like to know — it's our file that would be wrong, not yours.

On training, four fit Woking squarely. PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator, which is the engine above with the workings shown. PWLB repayment structures, for the annuity-versus-maturity question that 6.7 turns on. After the S114: capitalisation & EFS. And for members, Recent S114 case studies, which is written for exactly the conversation a scrutiny committee has about a book this size. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
